Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Genial poets, pink-faced earnest wits— you have given the world some choice morsels, gobbets of language presented as one presents T-bone steak and Cherries Jubilee. Goodbye, goodbye, I don’t care if I never taste your fine food again, neutral fellows, seers of every side. Tolerance, what crimes are committed in your name. And you, good women, bakers of nicest bread, blood donors. Your crumbs choke me, I would not want a drop of your blood in me, it is pumped by weak hearts, perfect pulses that never falter: irresponsive to nightmare reality. It is my brothers, my sisters, whose blood spurts out and stops forever because you choose to believe it is not your business. Goodbye, goodbye, your poems shut their little mouths, your loaves grow moldy, a gulf has split the ground between us, and you won’t wave, you’re looking another way. We shan’t meet again— unless you leap it, leaving behind you the cherished worms of your dispassion, your pallid ironies, your jovial, murderous, wry-humored balanced judgment, leap over, un- balanced? ... then how our fanatic tears would flow and mingle for joy ...

# The Rejection of Detachment: An Analysis of Moral Urgency in the Face of Suffering

The speaker of this poem mounts a scathing critique against those who would meet human suffering with anything less than full emotional and moral engagement. Through a series of escalating rejections, the poem constructs an argument that neutrality itself becomes a form of complicity, and that only those willing to abandon measured objectivity can achieve genuine solidarity with the suffering.

## Against the "Genial Poets" and Polished Wits

The poem opens by dismissing "genial poets" and clever "wits"—those who traffic in elegant language and refined sentiment without ever risking genuine engagement with pain. These figures represent a kind of aesthetic cowardice: they can turn a beautiful phrase, construct a clever metaphor, or offer sympathetic-sounding words, but their craft remains fundamentally decorative. The speaker suggests that such polished language, however skillfully rendered, ultimately evades the raw, unmanageable reality of suffering. Wit and genius become forms of distance-keeping, ways of transforming horror into something aesthetically containable and therefore safe. The speaker implicitly demands a different kind of poetry—one willing to be ugly, urgent, and unresolved if that is what truth requires.

## The Indictment of Tolerance and Neutrality

From this rejection of aesthetic evasion, the poem moves to a more pointed political and moral charge: tolerance and neutrality are not virtues but enablers of atrocity. The speaker suggests that the celebrated capacity to "see both sides," to withhold judgment in the name of fairness or balance, functions in practice as a kind of moral abdication. When confronted with violence and injustice, refusing to take a side does not represent wisdom or maturity—it represents permission granted to perpetrators to continue their crimes unchallenged. The poem thus reframes neutrality not as an absence of action but as an active choice with consequences, one that allows terrible things to happen precisely because those who might object have chosen not to.

## The Critique of the "Good Women"

This critique of neutrality finds its most visceral expression in the poem's treatment of the "good women" who bake bread and donate blood. These figures perform undeniably decent acts—nurturing, charitable, life-sustaining gestures that would seem to place them beyond reproach. Yet the speaker turns this apparent goodness into an indictment. The very calmness of these women's hearts, their capacity to continue their charitable routines undisturbed, becomes evidence of a deeper failure: they remain untouched by the violent deaths of the speaker's "brothers" and "sisters." Their equanimity is not peace but a kind of insulation, a protective distance from suffering that allows them to do good in comfortable, controlled ways while remaining fundamentally unmoved by catastrophe. The poem suggests that true solidarity cannot coexist with such untroubled hearts; real connection to others' suffering should disturb, disrupt, and unbalance.

## The Unbridgeable Gulf

This sustained critique culminates in the image of an unbridgeable gulf that has opened between the speaker and all these figures—the clever poets, the tolerant moderates, the calm-hearted good women. This gulf represents more than disagreement; it signifies a fundamental divergence in how suffering is experienced and understood. On one side stands the speaker, marked by grief, anger, and unresolved pain over lost brothers and sisters. On the other stand those who maintain their balanced judgment, their measured responses, their careful neutrality—and crucially, who refuse even to acknowledge that this gulf exists. Their failure is compounded by this refusal of recognition: they do not simply occupy different emotional territory: they deny that any meaningful division has occurred at all, treating their detachment as simply the reasonable, default position rather than a choice with moral weight.

## A Conditional Hope for Reunion

Yet the poem does not end in pure condemnation. It closes with a conditional hope, however tenuous: if these neutral, balanced figures could relinquish their ironic distance—their protective posture of detached commentary and even-handed judgment—and instead "leap" across the gulf into passionate, unbalanced solidarity, then reunion might become possible. This is not a hope for compromise or middle ground, but for a genuine transformation: the abandonment of irony and balance in favor of full-throated, partisan grief and outrage. Should such a leap occur, the poem suggests, it would not produce mere reconciliation but something more profound—a joyful, tearful reunion, charged with the emotional intensity that neutrality had previously foreclosed. The conditional nature of this ending preserves the poem's critical edge even as it gestures toward possibility: the gulf remains real and painful, but it is not, perhaps, permanently unbridgeable, provided those on the other side are willing to give up the very qualities—balance, irony, calm—that the poem has spent its length condemning.
outputs.L4:
This poem stages a confrontation between the speaker and a class of people the speaker holds in contempt: the "neutral" poets who traffic in tidy, well-crafted verses, and the well-meaning citizens who offer sympathy as a kind of social performance rather than as genuine solidarity. From the outset, the tone is accusatory rather than plaintive. The speaker does not plead with these figures to change; instead, the poem functions almost as an indictment, delivered in the second person, so that the addressed parties cannot hide behind the abstraction of "some people" or "society." They are named, called out, and made to answer for their complicity in a violence they claim to deplore while doing nothing to interrupt it.

The polished words these poets and citizens produce are treated as a kind of currency that has gone bad—language exchanged for comfort rather than truth. The poem's imagery makes this rot literal: food that has spoiled, blood that has been tainted, bodies and substances that should nourish or vitalized instead disgust and endanger. This visceral pairing of the abstract (empty rhetoric, hollow sympathy) with the physical (rotten food, poisoned blood) works to strip away the veneer of civility that "neutrality" wears. The poem suggests that to remain neutral in the face of suffering is not a passive or innocent position; it is an active participation in decay, a willingness to let the wound fester rather than to name it, tend it, or bleed alongside it.

The gestures of comfort offered by these figures—soft words, sympathetic nods, perhaps ritual expressions of concern—are exposed as false generosity. They cost the giver nothing and demand nothing of them in return; they are, in the speaker's eyes, transactions designed to preserve the giver's own comfort and moral self-image rather than to actually alleviate anyone's pain. The bitterness of the address comes precisely from this recognition: the speaker has seen through the performance and refuses to be soothed by it. Where the citizens and poets might expect gratitude or at least acknowledgment for their concern, they receive instead a kind of scornful unmasking.

This unmasking culminates in farewell—a valediction that is not tender but final. The speaker's goodbye is not a temporary parting but a declaration that the relationship, whatever bond of shared humanity or shared purpose once existed, has been irreparably broken. The rupture is presented as the direct consequence of the addressees' choice to remain neutral, to hover above the fray with ironic detachment rather than descend into the mess of real engagement. Irony itself becomes suspect here: the ironic stance, so often prized in literary and intellectual circles as a marker of sophistication, is recast as a form of cowardice, an "unbalanced complacency" that allows one to comment on suffering without ever risking anything for it.

Yet the poem does not close the door entirely. Embedded within its harsh farewell is a conditional possibility: if these bystanders were to abandon their ironic remove, if they set aside the comfortable equilibrium that lets them observe atrocity from a safe emotional distance, then something like reconciliation might still be possible. The poem gestures toward a shared grief that could unite speaker and addressee—but only on the far side of a genuine reckoning, only after the neutral parties surrender the very posture that has made them targets of the speaker's scorn. In this way, the poem holds together two seemingly incompatible impulses: an uncompromising rejection of false sympathy and complicit silence, and a residual hope that authentic solidarity, however unlikely, remains conceivable if only those addressed would finally choose to feel rather than merely to observe.

# Cherries Jubilee: A Genial Dessert for Any Occasion

There's something wonderfully genial about Cherries Jubilee, a dessert that combines theatrical flair with comforting sweetness. This classic dish, believed to have been created for Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee in 1887, has remained a beloved finale to elegant dinners for well over a century.

The preparation itself is a delightful spectacle. Fresh or pitted cherries are gently simmered in a sugar syrup, often enhanced with a touch of cinnamon or vanilla. The true magic happens tableside, where a generous splash of brandy or kirsch is added to the warm cherries, and then—with a genial flourish—the dish is set alight. Blue flames dance across the surface as the alcohol burns off, leaving behind a rich, complex flavor that beautifully complements the fruit's natural sweetness.

Traditionally served over vanilla ice cream, Cherries Jubilee creates a delightful contrast between warm, spiced fruit and cold, creamy indulgence. The combination is simple yet sophisticated, making it perfect for both formal dinner parties and casual family gatherings.

What makes this dessert particularly charming is its ability to bring people together. The flambéing process naturally draws attention and conversation, creating a genial atmosphere among guests as they watch the brief but captivating display. It transforms dessert from a mere course into a shared experience, a moment of communal delight.

Whether prepared by a professional chef in a fine restaurant or attempted by an adventurous home cook, Cherries Jubilee remains a testament to how a few quality ingredients, combined with a touch of showmanship, can create something truly memorable. It's a dessert that celebrates not just cherries, but the joy of sharing good food with good company.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a passionate free-verse poem titled "Goodbye to Tolerance" that condemns poets and everyday people for their neutrality and passivity in the face of violence and injustice.
counterfactuals.output:
# Goodbye to Tolerance

I am done with the poets who set their tables
with careful words, who season injustice
with a pinch of nuance and call it wisdom.

I am done with "on the other hand"
when the other hand is holding a knife.
I am done with balance
when one side of the scale
is a child's body
and the other is an excuse.

Goodbye to the shrug dressed up as philosophy.
Goodbye to the poem that ends in a question mark
when it should end in a fist through glass.
Goodbye to the workshop voice that says
*show, don't tell*
while the house burns down outside the window
and we're all still discussing craft.

I have watched neighbors
water their lawns
while three streets over
someone's whole life became rubble,
and I have said nothing,
and that nothing
was its own kind of violence,
green and growing
and watered every evening at six.

We built a religion out of *both sides*
and forgot which side we were kneeling on.
We call it maturity, this looking away.
We call it civility, this soft applause
for whoever speaks last and loudest
regardless of what they said.

I am tired of poets
who polish their doubt like a family heirloom,
who mistake the fog in their own chest
for depth,
who write *it's complicated*
about a boot on someone's neck.

It is not complicated.
It has never once been complicated.
The complication is a luxury
purchased with someone else's suffering,
paid for in the currency of silence
that we tell ourselves is patience,
is wisdom,
is peace.

I want a poetry that names names.
I want a citizenry that isn't furniture.
I want to stop mistaking my comfort
for a form of ethics.

So goodbye—
to the tolerance that tolerates everything
except the people being crushed,
to the poem that flinches from its own anger,
to the good, quiet people
who will explain to you, calmly,
why they didn't do anything,
while the fire
is still
burning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a bitter, accusatory poem addressed to "well-meaning" writers and ordinary citizens who refuse to take sides, using imagery of food, bread, and blood to symbolize false comfort and complicity.
counterfactuals.output:
# To Those Who Set the Table

You break your bread so carefully,
dividing crust from crumb,
as if the choice of which to eat
could keep the reckoning numb.

You call it balance, this soft refusal,
this buttering of both sides of the knife—
while somewhere else the wheat you praise
grows red, grows red, from someone's life.

I've watched you write your gentle verses,
your odes to "seeing every view,"
as if the blood soaked in the harvest
was just another point of view.

You sit at tables set with silence,
you pass the salt, you pass the blame,
you say "it's complicated" sweetly,
and complicated stays the same.

The wine you sip was pressed from something—
ask the grapes who did the press.
But no, you'd rather taste the vintage
and call your thirst a kind of rest.

I know your kind: the well-fed watchers,
who find all shouting in bad taste,
who'd rather starve a thousand voices
than let one meal go to waste.

You feed yourselves on both-sides pity,
you butter guilt to make it go down smooth,
but bread that's kneaded in indifference
still rises with the shape of proof.

So keep your table, keep your manners,
keep the plate you've licked of blame—
but don't call silence *nourishment*,
and don't call cowardice a *name*.

The hungry know which bread is poisoned.
The bleeding know which hands stayed clean
by never touching what was breaking,
by never choosing what they'd seen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: In the style of Denise Levertov, write a poem that says farewell to moderation and balanced judgment, accusing detached intellectuals of being complicit in the suffering of others.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Word to the Reasonable**

Goodbye to the middle distance,
to the careful weighing,
scale balanced on its pin
while the world tips
into fire.

I have loved you, moderation—
your cool hand,
your habit of seeing
both sides of the wound.

But there are those
who study the wound
as if it were a poem
requiring the right word,
who hold their tongues
the way one holds
a rare object, afraid
to chip the glaze.

I have sat in rooms
with such people. Intelligent.
Kind, even. They spoke
of complexity
while somewhere
a child's hand
was not being held
by anyone at all.

Their eyes were clear pools.
Nothing entered them
that could not be reflected on
at leisure, later,
over wine.

They are not evil.
That is the terrible thing—
they are only
careful,
and carefulness
has a price
paid by someone else,
always,
in another currency:
blood,
or bread withheld,
or the long silence
after the door
is broken down.

I say goodbye now
to the balanced sentence,
the both/and,
the on-the-other-hand.
Some hands
have only one gesture left:
to reach,
or to refuse to reach.

I choose the reaching,
badly made,
unbalanced,
alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a raw, emotional free verse piece where the speaker angrily bids goodbye to "neutral" poets and kind but indifferent people, using repeated phrases like "goodbye, goodbye" and vivid metaphors of blood, bread, and severed connection.
counterfactuals.output:
# Goodbye, Goodbye

Goodbye to the poets who write of moons
and never once mention whose boot is on whose neck.
Goodbye to your careful adjectives,
your therapeutic silences,
your poems about gardens
while the gardener is being shot
in the row behind the roses.

Goodbye, goodbye —
I am done translating my hunger
into language soft enough for your table.

You who are *kind* —
I have seen your kindness,
how it hands out bread
but will not ask who baked it,
who starved to knead it,
whose hands cracked open
so yours could stay soft.
You feed me and call it enough.
You feed me and look away
from the field where the wheat grew red,
where the water in the furrows
was not water.

Goodbye to your neutrality,
that clean white room
you built between your heart and mine,
so tidy, so ventilated,
so far from the smell of it —
the copper smell,
the smell that doesn't wash from language
no matter how many times
you rinse your verbs.

I don't want your prayers
that face every direction at once
so they can't be accused of praying wrong.
I don't want your silence
dressed up as wisdom.
I don't want your "both sides"
poured over the wound
like it was oil, like it could heal.

Goodbye, goodbye —
to the ones who loved me
in the abstract,
who wept at the idea of me
but not at the sound of my name
being erased from a map.

I am cutting the thread now.
Not because I don't bleed —
because I bleed *too much*
to keep handing you the needle
and asking you, please,
just this once,
sew something shut.

Goodbye to the bread you did not question.
Goodbye to the blood you did not name.
Goodbye to the goodbye
I keep having to say
because you keep almost — almost —
almost hearing me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a politically charged poem that rejects tolerance and detachment as forms of moral cowardice, ending with an image of a divide that can only be healed through shared grief and solidarity.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Line We Draw

They tell us to be reasonable,
to hold both truths like coins
in the same closed fist—
as if cruelty and its victim
deserve equal weight on the scale,
as if silence were a kind of wisdom
and not the oldest complicity.

I have grown tired of the word *tolerance*,
how it asks so little,
how it lets us stand at a distance
and call that distance peace.
Tolerance is the art of watching
without flinching.
It is not love. It is not courage.
It is the coward's translation of both.

Somewhere a child learns
that hunger is a policy decision.
Somewhere a mother memorizes
the names of the dead
like a rosary she never chose to hold.
And we—we debate the tone
of the emergency,
whether outrage is *productive*,
whether grief has a proper volume.

Detachment is not neutral.
It is a knife
that has simply decided
not to feel the wound it makes.

I will not applaud the fence-sitters,
the ones who call injustice *complicated*
because complexity is easier
than the plain, unbearable fact
of who is bleeding
and who is holding the blade.

There is a line now,
cut deep into the land
of what we were,
and no clever argument will close it,
no bipartisan silence,
no careful, comfortable middle.

Only this:
that we stand at the edge of it together,
not to argue whose side is right,
but to weep—
openly, without shame—
for everyone it has already swallowed.

Only grief, shared and unguarded,
can reach across that broken ground.
Only the willingness to break
in front of one another
can build the bridge
that reason never could.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
